narrative.text: The office is finally quiet. The last inauguration reception ended two hours ago. The staff has gone home. Outside the window, Republic Square is empty except for the street cleaners in their orange vests, sweeping up confetti and campaign leaflets. The silence feels enormous after the noise of the day — a cathedral of quiet where every sound is amplified. A knock at the door. Not Vyktor's knock. Softer. Serida Valk.

Serida enters with a newspaper tucked under her arm. She does not sit. She does not smile — she rarely smiles on duty — but there is something in her face that makes you put down your pen. Concern. Not alarm. Not yet. But concern.
One detail. Probably nothing. The Thornfeld Gazette ran a piece this morning predicting your BNI decision before you had made it.

She places the clipping on your desk. It is the morning edition, page four. The headline is unremarkable — 'New Chancellor Expected to Review Security Services' — but the body text contains specifics. Not guesses. Specifics. The names of two BNI directors who were discussed in your private meeting with Vyktor yesterday. The meeting no one else attended.
Probably a lucky guess. A reporter with good sources. It happens. I wanted you to see it.

She does not elaborate. But she does not take the clipping back either. She leaves it on your desk, beside your pen, like a small stone someone has placed on a path — easy to step over, impossible to unsee once you have noticed it.

Serida does not bring me things that are 'probably nothing.' She brings me things that might be something and wants me to decide which. Two years as head of personal security — she knows the difference between a leak and a journalist doing their job. The question is which one this is. I will find out. Maybe not today. But I will find out.
